findings.claim: The two o1 items present method-signature shorthand such as total(int a, int b) as complete methods, so a literal reader can conclude no option is a compilable declaration and the single unambiguous key is undermined.
findings.recommendation: Keep the concepts, counts and answers, but call the options method signatures and state that return types and bodies are omitted.

findings.claim: Both o2 items test boundary inputs only; no item requires an ordinary case, an invalid case, a complete three-kind test set or an expected result, although the objective requires all of them.
findings.recommendation: Replace one boundary item with a scenario requiring an ordinary, a boundary and an invalid input with expected results or an explicit result-checking step; keep two o2 items with four options.

findings.claim: The credited count(n + 1) feedback says the base case is unreachable from 1, while the wraparound distractor feedback says n can come back around to 0 but the stack runs out first, so option feedback is mutually inconsistent.
findings.recommendation: Keep the scenario, key and wraparound distractor; change only the credited feedback to say the base case is not reached before the call stack runs out.

findings.claim: After the Step Over breakpoint caveat, the unbounded first o2 stem lets Step Over also enter helper when an enabled breakpoint exists there, so the item no longer guarantees one key.
findings.recommendation: Keep the options and caveat, but state that no breakpoint is set inside helper and ask which stepping control directly enters it.
